This year we’ve had a clear jump in model capability where instead of telling agents precisely what to do, it’s better to use these systems to solve problems you can’t easily define yourself. 

A year ago you’d need to very clearly tell agents the how to design and develop your product idea, or there was almost no chance of success. Now, increasingly, the agent likely can come up with a better implementation than you’d have thought of because you can have it connect the dots between a far greater solution space than you can. 

This will be increasingly true in basically every domain of kneeler work. We’re going to see this impact in finance, legal, life sciences, cyber, and many other spaces where no person can hold onto all the available relevant industry knowledge to think of the best solution. 

Ultimately this is going to reshape our relationship with AI and how we deploy agents in our work. It won’t be about explicitly telling them, but instead giving them goals and enough freedom to pursue them in the best way they can.

podcasts.name: Latent Space
podcasts.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
podcasts.transcript:
Kari writing this blog post, like issue tracking is dead. Yeah.

So like how do you explain to your customers that like, "Hey, you know, our entire business was issue tracking before, and now our CEO just wrote this blog post"?

The great thing about our business is that we're not like so big to like kill ourselves, right? [laughs] Yeah. Like [laughs] um- [laughs]...

it's probably really hard if you're Google to like kill the search business, right? Yeah. And put an AI, you know, box at the top of every search result, and maybe no one's gonna look at the ads, right?

So your entire business is upended. And like yes, the unit of the issue still exists, but we probably shouldn't have a world where people are like manually tracking work. Yeah. So like that's what's dead, right?

So in a lot of cases when we were talking to various customers as this, you know, blog post came out, most of our customers were like, "Yeah." [laughs] "Issue tracking is dead. And by the way, like, what are you guys?

What am I buying?" [laughs] Right? [upbeat music] Christina Cordova, you're the COO of Linear. Could you introduce yourself? Yeah, yeah. So I'm Christina.

Um, I've been at Linear for about three and a half years now, joined as COO, and I'm still COO today.

Prior to Linear, I spent time at Notion leading our platform, so the build-out of our APIs, and then our partnerships and self-serve growth initiatives as well.

And then before that, I was at Stripe for seven and a half years, and there I led a lot of our early partnerships and go-to-market, um, and then moved over to the product side and built out some new products for early-stage companies.

So I've been probably anywhere from like the product side of a company and like managing engineers all the way to, uh, managing, you know, the business side of a company as well, um, which has been really fun.

So why did Linear hire a COO at like 40 employees? Is that like odd- [laughs]... or is that pretty normal? Um, I mean, I, I generally don't believe every company needs a COO. Yeah. Right?

Like when I talk to founders and they're like, "Hey, like I think I've found product market fit. Like how do we start to scale like the business side of the company?"

I am often I feel like cautioning against maybe hiring someone like me. [laughs] Yeah. So I think for every company it's a little bit different.

I think you have to really understand as like a founder, like what are the things you need and what are the things you're looking for in the people that you bring onto the team?

Often early on it's just like I need someone to like sell something, right? [laughs] Uh, we have expanded beyond the capability of the founder or CEO to sell every net new customer, right?

So there I generally talk about, well, you should hire folks in sales, maybe hire a sales leader- Yeah... to build out a team, right?

But if you're not exactly sure what you're looking for in like marketing or operations or other parts of the company, um, then it may very well not make sense to hire someone like me.

You know, I think with the Linear founders, um, you know, they were incredibly focused on like design and engineering and product, um, and I think they had a really great, you know, kind of combination of skills between the three of them.

But as we were starting to scale the business side of the company, they didn't necessarily look at like the next salesperson that we hired and said, "Hmm, I know exactly what we're looking for here, and I know whether or not sales is performing really well," right?

So if you don't look at different parts of your company and say like, "Okay, I know what great is, and I feel like I have a good sense of like how to get to great," it can sometimes be helpful to hire someone like me or like a functional leader, like when it comes time to do that.

Yeah, so like what did the business look like at that point? Like can you talk about like what revenue they were at or... Yeah, we were probably,

I wanna say, you know, we had some large customers but no like public company customers. Yeah. Uh, probably no customer above, I wanna say, like maybe 500 seats or something like that.

So I would say like m- we mostly tapped out at like mid-market, and we were probably best well known for being a great product for startups, but not necessarily a great product for other companies- Yeah... at that time.

Um, you know, and I think at that point in time, we were, we're doing well with like a product-led growth model- Mm... where most people were using our product because they signed up self-serve. Mm.

Um, and then grew with us over time. So companies like Vercel and Ramp and many other customers like that, you know, really never talked to a human being, um, at Linear.

Signed up for the product, started using it, and then started scaling, which was great. Like you know the product can do a lot of work on its own. Yeah.

But it was also star- like time to start selling to, you know, the company that is not even gonna put like a lick of data into your service without, you know, signing a contract- Yeah...

and doing a pilot and, uh, surveying their team on, you know, what tool they were using before and what to, you know, what tool is this and what's better, right?

Um, so that was a very different kind of motion for the company to start scaling to larger, uh, companies, and that was like pretty much my objective. Um, and we've at least 10Xed, I think, since I joined. Nice. So.

And you joined like four years ago? Uh, three, almost three and a half years ago, yeah. Oh, okay. So I think the Linear founders have talked about this.

I think you have as well, that like w- before you join Linear you always do a, like a trial period. Yes. So did you also have to do- Yes... a trial period? I did. Okay. Yeah, yeah. So yeah, like what was that like?

Yeah, I mean, I think my project was quite simple. It was something like, uh, you know, come up with the go-to-market plan for Linear, you know, with a bounded time period, like for the next six to 12 months- Yeah...

or something like that, right? And I think the good thing about that is that, you know, that is the job, [laughs] like right? Yeah.

So you're not giving someone some like fictional project that's not really like representative of like what they would do when they join the company.

It's like a real, uh, project, and that would, you know, effectively be my job in joining the company. So- Yeah... you know, if they didn't like the outcomes that I produced- [laughs]...

as part of that project, they probably, you know, shouldn't hire me. Yeah.

Um, so I think it was a really good way of saying like, "I have some ideas of what the company can do better, but also I wanna like get feedback from the people who are on the ground."

Like, you know, we had a salesperson on our team. We had someone doing customer success. Uh, we had some people doing support, and, you know, one or two folks doing marketing, right?

Um, so kind of getting their perspectives on different parts of the business and, like, where I should focus and where to, where to prioritize, and then making sure that, like, the company was also bought in on, like, that vision for the world, uh, was, I think, really helpful for me.

And then when I actually started at the company, it was almost like I had this little blueprint- Yeah... for, you know, what my job should be and what I should accomplish. Can you talk about, like, what was in that plan?

[laughs] Um, I think a, a lot of it was, like, brand and marketing oriented, so like, you know, things around, like, making Linear inevitable, um, in a lot of ways.

So, you know, either you're already on Linear, or you should be, like, planning your move to Linear [laughs] effectively. Yeah.

Um, and most companies that we want to acquire should be, you know, in, you know, one world or the other.

So a lot of that was around, you know, driving the brand, building storytelling, uh, uh, I think increasing awareness for the company, 'cause I think we were...

We were well known, but I would say in, like, particular niches- Yeah... not really outside- Like startups... of that. Yeah. Okay.

Um, so it's like, you know, we were doing marketing, but, like, the only marketing that we were doing was, like, sending out emails if we, like, had a change log of something new that we released. Yeah.

And it turns out that, like, less than 10% of users, like, subscribed to emails, so most people didn't necessarily know even just, like, the new features we were- Yeah... shipping, which was interesting.

Um, and then we would, like, send a tweet. [laughs] Okay. Like, from- Um, from- From the founder's accounts or, like, from the company account? From, from the company account. Okay.

[laughs] And then, and then, you know, the founders would re- reshare and, you know, they have their own, like, pretty strong, like, social presence as well. Yeah. But, you know, that was, like, the extent of it really.

Yeah. Like, um, so, you know, a lot of it was just thinking about, okay, like, how are we telling a more holistic story in a better way? And then how are we actually reaching the people that we want to be reaching?

It turns out that, like, actually, a lot of our users are, like, in the app, you know, day to day. Yeah.

And so, like, why are we not just, like, giving them notifications about, like, what's changing within the product, like, within the place they're already at every day? Yeah. Right?

Um, so, you know, just thinking about things that could be great ways to market to existing users or market to, like, net new customers that also didn't feel, like, off with the brand, right? Yeah.

So I spent a lot of time on that. Um, a lot of it was also just, like, growing the sales team.

You know, I think a lot of early stage companies especially that are, like, engineering driven, like, product-led growth oriented are like, "You know, the product should sell itself."

And then everyone realizes, like, well, that gets you to a certain point. Yeah.

[laughs] And then when you want to, like, grow faster, right, um, you also need to start thinking about, um, reaching people in different ways, and not everyone buys products self-serve.

And especially when you're choosing a system that's, like, so core to, like, your product development process, which we are- Yeah... um,

a lot of companies are not going to make that decision without, like, building trust with human beings. Um, and you know, when I was doing my work trial, we had, like, one person on sales, right?

Uh, so- That was not you. [laughs] So it was just like, you know, there's, there's only so much you could do with, like, one person, right? And were they, like, an experienced salesperson? Yeah. Oh, okay.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah. Um, he's actually our sales leader today. Oh, okay. Cool. So leads our entire sales team, so he's great. Um, but, uh, you know, at the time, I would say this wasn't really on him.

It was more on the company. It's just like, how do we actually think we wanna grow this team, right? You can grow a sales team in lots of ways. You can have, like, lots of SDRs. Mm-hmm. We don't have any SDRs.

You can have forward deployed engineers now. That's very popular, right? We actually don't do, uh, forward deployed engineering.

We have solutions engineers, uh, which I, you know, think is distinct and somewhat different, uh, but we added those later. We really- And that's part of the sales org? Yeah. Cool.

Uh, we really optimized our team at the beginning for hiring, um, AEs who had experience, like, selling technical products, um, because we knew, like, if you had sold to a designer, if you had sold to an engineer before,

we wouldn't necessarily have to teach you how to do that. And I think selling to someone who's, like, very discerning, doesn't wanna see your fancy slides, just wants to get into a demo- Yeah...

you know, is very different from selling to, like, a person in, I don't know, people ops or, you know, something else.

So, um, looking for people with that, like, very explicit experience and then, um, making sure that we could, like, onboard them and train them and get them, like, really competent in the product itself- Yeah...

um, because that's required to build trust with our customer, right?

So just figuring out, like, what's different about this company and what's going to be different about hiring or scaling, you know, and also, like, what's the way that the founders wanna do it, and, like, can we do that?

So support is an interesting example. When I was interviewing, the founders were very clear that, like, they did not wanna outsource support, and I've never worked at a company that didn't- Yeah... outsource support.

[laughs] So that was like, okay. Wait, I thought Stripe does it internally, right? No. Oh. They out- they outsource. Oh, okay. Yeah. Interesting. Um, unless something's changed, uh- [laughs]...

since I was there, but, you know, they have internal folks who work on support too. Yeah. Um, but they do outsource.

So, you know, I think for us, uh, that was something that we really wanted to maintain because we really cared about, like, delivering a high-quality experience, delivering a fast experience, and knowing that for a long time we didn't have a sales team, right?

Yeah. So because we didn't have that, we knew that your first touchpoint, often, if you wanted to talk to a human being, was going to be support, so the support better be good. Yeah. Right?

Um, and so we've still been able to figure out how to scale the team today, um, into, like, a global team that does not outsource at all. Um, so, you know, we'll see what the future brings. [laughs] Yeah.

You know, uh, never say never on any of these things.

Um, but, you know, there are certain ways that we wanna do things, and we probably wanna do them for, like, as long as possible, as long, as long as it's, like, feasible for the business and makes sense. Yeah.

So when you first joined, like, I guess I've never been in a sales role, but, like, do you have to say, "Okay, we're starting with startups, and we can't just immediately go to, like, big enterprises and start selling them."

Yeah. "We have to, like, kinda go step by step"? So, like, did you have to go, "Oh, we have to first get, like, medium-sized businesses, and then at some point we'll go enterprise"? Like, how does that work? Yeah, yeah.

So when I joined Linear, I think we had, like, three goals, like, three company-level goals, and I think one of them was, like, move up market to enterprise.

And then we had, like, a company offsite three weeks after I joined, and I, like, got up in front of the whole company, which was, like, I don't know, 35, 40 people at the time, and, like, I showed the slide of the three goals, and I, like, crossed the, like, one that says, "We're gonna go after enterprises out."

Okay. Because I was like, "We have one person." Yeah. "We have literally one person on sales." Like, you know [laughs] you're not going upmarket to enterprise with one person. Yeah. Like [laughs] you know?

So you have to think about, like, what are you capable of doing? Uh, what do you need to, like, learn in order to, to get there? And then, do you actually have the resources to, like, accomplish that goal, right?

And, you know, I, I don't think we had any of those things at that period of time. Yeah. Right?

We had companies that we had primarily won because they had scaled into being, like, a growth stage business or, like, a mid-market business, effectively.

But we hadn't done a lot of, like, acquiring net new, like, mid-market companies at that point.

So I changed that goal to say, like, "No, we're gonna go after, like, companies in the growth segment, and that's gonna be our goal."

And if we can win a lot of companies who are in the growth segment, who already have, like, a tool, um, that does, in some ways, what we do, and we, we have to go in, and we have to convince them to, like, rip that out and replace it with Linear, then if we're able to do that, that gives me the confidence to say that, you know, in a year or in two years we're gonna be able to go after enterprises.

But, like, I don't have confidence in that now, so why would I set that as a goal for the team? Yeah. Um, so completely agree.

It's, like, really about setting those baby steps and making sure that, like, you're doing well with companies that you can serve today incredibly well so that those companies, when they're doing, like, you know, they're getting, like, the reference calls from the larger companies, being like, "Hey," like, "do you like Linear, and has your experience been good?"

They're saying, like, really positive things. Um, and that helps us land, like, the net new customer. And, like, it worked very similarly when I was at Stripe.

Like, we did not win a lot of, like, net new companies that were switching over from a competitor- Yeah... for a long time. Uh, we did a great job, like, winning every net new businesses that, that was created. Mm-hmm.

So, like, a startup- Yeah... that's implementing payments for the first time. Um, and then we kind of started to win companies who were switching over. Um, and some of that stuff just takes time.

It's very, like, it's very different to sell a product where you have to rip technology out that already exists- Mm...

and replace it than just to sell something that's, like, nice and shiny and new on top of, like, an existing set of systems. Yeah.

So knowing that I was in, like, a very similar position in this role, uh, it was important that, like, I just oriented the team around, like, what I felt was, like, a solvable problem.

And then only in 2025, so that was 2023, only in 2025 did I, you know, go up in front of a company and say, like, "We're going after enterprise this year," right? Oh, wow.

And that was when we started our enterprise sales segment and built out that team. Yeah. So okay, you guys are going, like, medium-sized businesses, and so you are getting everyone to basically, like...

'Cause most pe- most companies have an issue tracker, right? Yep. Or- Or some kind of- Yeah... tool to track their work. And so you have to try to, like- Yeah... rip them away from them.

So yeah, like, how do you convince them to say, "Oh yeah, we're using XYZ product. It works for us, but, uh," yeah, like, you know, pitch me, basically. [laughs] Yeah. Why should I switch it? In the- Yeah...

in the early days it was about being, like, significantly better- Yeah... than what the alternative solutions were. Okay. Right? I don't think you can be, like, 20% better, 30% better- Yeah...

and get people to switch, 'cause there's a switching cost involved, right?

So I think you have to figure out how you articulate how your product is better than what is already, like, serving the market reasonably well, reasonably well enough to, that they have, like, a lot of companies that are using their product, right?

Th- but the good thing about the space that we were entering, and I think one of the reasons why, like, the Linear founders chose this space were because they were all users of those legacy tools- Yeah... right?

Uh, when they were working at, like, Coinbase and Airbnb and Uber. And so they knew, like, no one liked [laughs] these tools, right? Yeah, yeah.

And when they were getting rolled out, like, at their companies, they were like, "Oh, no," like, you know, "the fun time is going away. We have to start- Yeah... using these tools," right?

So, um, y- in a lot of ways it really helped that they had this, like, knowledge and existing awareness of, like, the feeling that came with the competitors in our space. Yeah.

And could figure out how to build a product that got people really excited, like, to manage their work, right? Mm-hmm. Which is presumably not something that you would expect.

So a lot of the emphasis in what we built early on was in, like, design and UX, right? Yeah. Make it a product that people want to be in every day and have to use.

The hard part about that is that people have to, like, try it before they get it, right? Yeah. Versus, like, seeing a couple slides in a sales deck and being like, "Okay," like- Yeah... "I get it," right?

So one of the things that we did, I think very well strategically, was just having a product that anyone could start using, so you know, a free product initially, um, that once you hit certain limits in terms of usage, you would have to start paying for.

So a lot of people who started to use Linear for their company, um, actually were just playing around with it for their own purposes for free and got a sense of, like, how usable it was and how much easier it would be, um, to utilize the product compared to competitors.

Um, so we started very much there, and I think that worked well for a period of time. Now our approach in terms of, like, how we sell Linear is very different.

We're typically talking to companies about the sea change in the space, um, that has happened over the last year and a half- Yeah...

two years in terms of, like, you know, your entire, like, product development process has been upended. Mm-hmm. The way that you build products has completely changed, and

it doesn't make sense anymore to live in a world where you are, like, you have, like, a manual way of saying like, "Oh," like, "I found a bug. Oh, I'm going to, like, report that bug into my issue tracker." Yeah.

"Oh, I'm going to label it and assign it to this other person, and then that person is going to fix it," and, you know, add a status update, and then close it, [laughs] and then, like, notify the customer.

And every step in that path is, like, completely manual. Um, that's just, it doesn't make any sense for the world that we live in now, and you talk to most companies, and they're like, "Yes." [laughs] Yeah.

"I completely agree." Um, and so we've really oriented the company in the last year and a half around agents and agents performing a lot of the parts of the workflow that are effectively not product development.
